questions.q: What is the key difference between a one-way chat notification and true ChatOps for a security alert?
options: There is no real difference; both terms describe the exact same thing
A notification can only be sent to Teams, never to Slack
ChatOps means the message is sent by email instead of chat
ChatOps requires putting an interactive action, like an Approve button, directly in the message, which needs a receiving endpoint back into your automation; a notification only needs to be sent out
questions.explain: Notification is push-only; ChatOps adds a second channel back in, since the chat platform must tell your automation which button was clicked, requiring a receiving endpoint like the one built in Lesson 17.

questions.q: What format does the Teams example in this lesson use to post a formatted alert through an incoming webhook?
options: A raw HTML email template
An Adaptive Card, Teams' declarative JSON card layout
Slack's Block Kit format
A plain unformatted text string only
questions.explain: Teams renders a JSON Adaptive Card sent via an incoming webhook into a formatted message with text blocks and fact sets.

questions.q: Why can a Slack message sent through a plain incoming webhook display real buttons but still fail to deliver the button click back to your code?
options: A plain incoming webhook is push-only; receiving the click requires a registered Slack app with an interactivity endpoint configured to receive the POST when a button is clicked
Slack buttons are purely decorative and never clickable
Buttons require the message to be sent over email instead of a webhook
Slack does not support buttons in Block Kit at all
questions.explain: The webhook can push a message with buttons, but telling your code about a click requires a separate interactivity endpoint tied to a registered Slack app.

questions.q: In verify_slack_request(), what does the timestamp check (rejecting requests older than 5 minutes) protect against?
options: It prevents the signing secret from ever expiring
It automatically escalates any ticket older than 5 minutes
It protects against replay of an old, previously captured request being resent later
It has no security purpose and is only used for logging
questions.explain: Combining a timestamp into the signed basestring and rejecting old timestamps is replay protection — an old captured request can't be resent later and still pass verification.

questions.q: What must happen before a handler acts on which Slack button (action_id) was clicked, according to this lesson?
options: Nothing — Slack guarantees every interaction request is authentic by default
The request must pass verify_slack_request's signing-secret and timestamp checks before the handler trusts which action_id was clicked or calls functions like escalate_ticket
The analyst must re-type the alert's event_id manually into Slack
The ticket must already be closed before any button click is processed
questions.explain: The approval button is cosmetic until the request behind it is verified — the same principle as webhook signature verification, applied to a button click.
